questions_now.q: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?
Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?

lines_now.short: In a Johns Hopkins study, most volunteers given psilocybin scored as having a 'complete' mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines_now.but: Everyone in the psilocybin study took part in religious or spiritual activities; the authors say that may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.
'Mystical' meant high questionnaire scores for unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.
Two months after psilocybin, most said it had changed them for the better; people close to them saw small changes. Personality and mood tests didn't.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.
lines_now.rate: The lasting part comes from one study of 24 religious or spiritual volunteers rating their own psilocybin sessions. Another trial found high scores during sessions, but almost everyone guessed which pill they got.

freq.what: volunteers ranked their psilocybin session among the 5 most meaningful experiences of their lives, 2 months later
compare: after methylphenidate (a stimulant used for comparison)
freq.note: One study: 16 of 24 after psilocybin, 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (counted from a figure). All took part in religious or spiritual activities.

claim.statement: In 36 healthy volunteers in Baltimore who had never used hallucinogens and who all took part at least now and then in religious or spiritual activities (Griffiths et al., 2006; 20 daily and 14 at least monthly; mean age 46; 14 men; 35 college graduates; recruited with community flyers about a study of states of consciousness and a substance used sacramentally in some cultures, and unpaid), psilocybin given by the study under supportive conditions (trial conditions: a capsule of 30 mg/70 kg by mouth in an 8-hour session alone with two monitors in a living-room-like room, lying down with an eye mask and classical music, after four preparation meetings of 8 hours in all whose stated expectation was that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight), compared within the same people with methylphenidate (40 mg/70 kg), a stimulant chosen as an active comparison, the two sessions given 2 months apart in random order to 30 of them (15 per order), is associated with much higher scores on questionnaires of mystical experience about 7 hours after the capsule, and 2 months later with higher self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and well-being that the volunteers attributed to the session, a small positive change rated by people who knew them, and no detectable difference on personality or mood questionnaires. 'Mystical' here means questionnaire scores: on the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire, part of a 100-item questionnaire and based on Stace's descriptions of mystical experience, the seven scales (internal and external unity, transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, intuitive knowledge and deeply felt positive mood) averaged 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum after psilocybin against 0.21 to 0.38 after methylphenidate, and the 32-item Mysticism Scale total was 252.1 against 174.7 (all P < 0.001; means with standard errors, no intervals). A 'complete' mystical experience was defined in advance as at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six scales: 19 of the 30 met it in their blinded psilocybin session (10 of 15 in the first session and 9 of 15 in the second; 63 in 100, editors' sum), and the paper's headline figure, 22 of 36 (61%), adds 3 of the 6 decoy volunteers whose third session was open-label psilocybin; 4 of 36 met it after methylphenidate (2 in each of the first two sessions, which included the decoy volunteers' two methylphenidate sessions). The questionnaire on lasting effects, assembled for this study from earlier and new items and introduced after it had begun, was completed by 24 of the 30 (12 per order): 2 months after psilocybin, 16 of 24 (67 in 100) rated it the single most meaningful experience of their lives (3) or among the top five (13) (counts from Figure 3, editors' reading), against 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (top five; none the single most), and some likened its meaning to the birth of a first child or the death of a parent; 33% (8 of 24) rated it the single most spiritually significant experience of their lives and another 38% (9) among the top five, against 8% (2) after methylphenidate; 79% (19) said it had increased their well-being or life satisfaction moderately (50%) or very much (29%), against 17% (4) and 4% (1) after methylphenidate, and no one reported a decrease after either drug (counts out of 24 by editors' arithmetic). Mean ratings were 6.54 against 3.42 for personal meaning (1 to 8), 4.79 against 2.63 for spiritual significance (1 to 6) and +2.04 against +0.79 for change in well-being (−3 to +3) (each P < 0.001). Three adults named by each participant (relatives, friends or colleagues), interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session and told their own earlier ratings, rated a mean positive change of 2.42 after psilocybin against −0.03 after methylphenidate (26 participants analysed; P < 0.01), which the authors call small. The NEO PI-R personality inventory and the PANAS-X positive and negative affect scales showed no difference attributable to psilocybin (no values shown); lifetime mysticism and spiritual transcendence scores were higher after psilocybin, shown only in a figure without numbers. The experience was not uniformly pleasant: monitors rated higher peak anxiety or fearfulness during psilocybin sessions (1.05 against 0.42 on a 0 to 4 scale) as well as more joy (2.03 against 0.63) and peace (1.90 against 0.92); 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session as strong or extreme (none after methylphenidate); 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria, 4 of them for the whole session (6 of the 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count), and 6 of these 8 had transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking; these were managed with reassurance, no volunteer needed drug treatment, 2 compared the experience to being in a war and 3 said they would never want to repeat it, while most of the 8 still rated it as meaningful. The authors, who call this 31% with significant fear and 17% with transient ideas of reference or paranoia, warn that without monitoring such reactions could escalate to panic and dangerous behaviour. Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin; participants were never asked which drug they thought they had received; the monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate psilocybin, and the authors judged the blinding adequately maintained because the monitors still believed several drugs and placebo had been given. Three of the four commentaries published with the trial in the same issue, none with data of its own, read the monitors' errors in about a quarter of sessions as a sign of careful blinding (Kleber, 2006) or of results unlikely to reflect expectations (Snyder, 2006), or the stimulant comparison as showing effects beyond expectation (Schuster, 2006), although the participants themselves were never asked. The authors state that how far the results generalize is unknown and that the volunteers' religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritually significant reading of the experience more likely. In a separate randomized trial by another team, in 93 adults with alcohol dependence who were not selected for religious or spiritual practice (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; funded by the Heffter Research Institute, an NIH translational-science grant and private donors), mean total scores on the same 43-item questionnaire (0 to 1) were 0.59 after a first psilocybin session (25 mg/70 kg) against 0.10 after the antihistamine diphenhydramine as an active placebo, and 0.64 against 0.11 after the second session (both P < .001), with correct guesses of the medication after about 94 in 100 sessions (percentages without counts). Griffiths et al. was funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Council on Spiritual Practices, which two of its four authors list as an affiliation, and prints no conflict-of-interest statement. The 2-month ratings come from one study; its 1-year follow-up, under way in 2006, is reported only as bringing no mention of persisting perceptual effects or problematic recreational hallucinogen use in open interviews with 30 of 36. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the questionnaire scores during the session (two independent trials); the 2-month ratings rest on one study.
claim.population: 36 healthy, hallucinogen-naive adults in Baltimore (mean age 46, range 24 to 64; 14 men; 35 college graduates, 20 with postgraduate degrees) who all reported at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities (20 daily, 14 at least monthly), recruited by community flyers and unpaid, 30 of them in the blinded crossover (Griffiths et al., 2006); and, for the questionnaire scores during the session only, 93 treated adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence in a randomized trial at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (Bogenschutz et al., 2022)
claim.exposure: Psilocybin given by the study in individual 8-hour sessions under supportive conditions (trial conditions: 30 mg/70 kg by mouth after about 8 hours of preparation meetings, with two monitors, eye mask and music, in Griffiths et al.; 25 mg/70 kg, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg, by mouth within 12 psychotherapy sessions in Bogenschutz et al.)
claim.comparator: Methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth, an active stimulant, in the same people 2 months apart in random order (Griffiths et al.); diphenhydramine 50 mg, then 100 mg, as an active placebo in a parallel group with the same psychotherapy (Bogenschutz et al.)
claim.outcome: Mystical-experience questionnaire scores about 7 hours after the capsule (the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire within the States of Consciousness Questionnaire; the 32-item Mysticism Scale) and a predefined 'complete' mystical experience; 2 months later, self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and change in well-being or life satisfaction, ratings by three people who knew each participant, personality (NEO PI-R), affect (PANAS-X) and lifetime mysticism scores; fear, anxiety and ideas of reference during sessions
claim.magnitude: Griffiths et al. (2006), within-person, N=30, means (SEM): Mysticism Scale total 252.1 (8.5) against 174.7 (11.3); States of Consciousness Questionnaire scales 0.66 to 0.81 against 0.21 to 0.38 of the maximum; all P < 0.001, no intervals printed. Complete mystical experience: 19 of 30 in blinded psilocybin sessions (editors' sum of 10 of 15 and 9 of 15; exact 95% interval 44% to 80%, editors' calculation); 22 of 36 including 3 of 6 open-label sessions; 4 of 36 after methylphenidate. At 2 months (N=24): single most or top-five most meaningful 16 of 24 (67%; exact 95% interval 45% to 84%, editors' calculation) against 2 of 24; single most spiritually significant 33%, top five another 38%, against 8% top five; well-being increased moderately or very much 79% against 21% (17% and 4%); mean personal meaning 6.54 (0.22) against 3.42 (0.35), spiritual significance 4.79 (0.26) against 2.63 (0.22), change in well-being +2.04 (0.17) against +0.79 (0.18), each P < 0.001. Observers (N=26): mean positive change 2.42 (0.70) against −0.03 (0.68), P < 0.01. NEO PI-R and PANAS-X: no difference, values not shown. Strong or extreme fear 11 of 36 against none; notable anxiety or dysphoria 8 of 36 (6 of 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count). Bogenschutz et al. (2022), 48 against 45: mean MEQ total 0.59 (SD 0.24) against 0.10 (0.13) after session 1 and 0.64 (0.21) against 0.11 (0.16) after session 2, P < .001; correct guesses after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions.
claim.rating_reasoning: Randomized evidence (a crossover with drug order assigned at random, and a parallel-group trial) starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-rated outcomes, expectation, functional unblinding) and one for imprecision (24 people for the 2-month ratings): low. Rated as worded: much higher scores on mystical-experience questionnaires after psilocybin than after an active comparison, and, 2 months later, in volunteers selected for religious or spiritual practice, higher self-rated meaning and attributed change, a small change rated by people who knew them and no detectable change on personality or mood inventories; it does not say that psilocybin changes personality or that most people who take it have a mystical experience. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status replicated for the acute questionnaire effect only: Griffiths et al. (Johns Hopkins, against methylphenidate) and Bogenschutz et al. (New York University and the University of New Mexico, against diphenhydramine) are independent; the 2-month ratings, the comparison with a stimulant and the counts of 'complete' mystical experiences rest on Griffiths et al. alone, and the plain lines say 'one study' for them. The paper's headline counts pool the 30 blinded volunteers with 6 open-label sessions (22 of 36 complete mystical experiences, 11 of 36 strong fear, 8 of 36 notable anxiety); the claim gives the blinded count (19 of 30) beside them. Not used: the 14-month follow-up of these volunteers (Griffiths et al., 2008), known here only as cited by Johnson et al. (2014). The four commentaries published with the paper in the same issue (Nichols, 2006; Snyder, 2006; Schuster, 2006; Kleber, 2006), the published responses METHODS §2.3 asks for, have now been read in full: all four praise the trial and none reports data of its own, so they enter only as what they argue and change neither the certainty nor the replication status. Snyder, Kleber and Schuster treated expectation as controlled, from the monitors' errors or the stimulant comparison; participants were never asked to guess, and the risk-of-bias downgrade already counts this. Schuster also argued that the expectations set by the preparation and the introspective setting may be an important determinant of the experience, which the claim's wording for supportive conditions already reflects. The only harm figure in the four, Kleber's 8 of 36 volunteers with sessions dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, is the trial's own; Snyder calls adverse events very few, without numbers. Nichols, who synthesized the trial's psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 282), calls the trial placebo-controlled, although its comparison was an active drug; he is not entered. Funding and the funder affiliation of two authors are stated. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.

lines_now.short: Studies often found less low mood and stress than before, and more wellbeing; some people had headaches or slept badly.
lines_now.but: Most studies had no blinded placebo group, and most took place in labs or ceremonies with support, not at parties or at home.
how: A review collected 48 studies of psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca and similar drugs.
People filled in the same questionnaires before, and again in the days or weeks after.
Most studies that measured it found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, than before.
In studies that looked for problems, headaches were most common, and one person had a severe worsening of anxiety.
lines_now.rate: 48 studies, most without a dummy-pill comparison, in supportive settings. The review only counted which studies found a change, not how big, and side effects were reported unevenly.

claim.statement: In a systematic review of 48 studies (1,774 people) of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, mostly given in laboratories, clinical trials or ceremonies with preparation and aftercare (Evens et al., 2023; AMSTAR 2 critically low), measurements taken between one day and one month after use, compared with each person's own measurements before, most often showed less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness (changes reported in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured these), and no study found group-level worsening of mental health. Bad after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked for them: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with single cases of severe anxiety and of relapse to methamphetamine use. Half the studies had a control group of some kind, but only 14 of the 48 had a placebo group with double-blinding, only statistically significant results were counted, and half the studies did not say whether they looked for side effects, so the size and cause of these changes, and how often they happen with recreational use, are unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Adults, clinical and nonclinical, taking classic psychedelics in laboratory studies, clinical trials or ceremonies, in 48 studies gathered by a systematic review
claim.exposure: A session with psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline
claim.comparator: The same people's measurements before the session (a control group in 24 studies, placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14)
claim.outcome: Psychological measures and adverse effects between one day and one month after use
claim.magnitude: No effect sizes; counts of studies. Changes in 70 to 90% of studies measuring depression, stress and grief; mindfulness; personality and attitudes; wellbeing; social effects. Adverse events: assessed or mentioned in 25 of 48 studies (550 participants); none in 11 (297 participants); reported in 14 (253 participants): 52 headaches, 6 sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, single severe cases.
claim.rating_reasoning: Most included studies are pre–post or observational, so the evidence starts low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness to very low. Worded as an association with before-use measurements. Status replicated: many studies in the same direction for the main domains, though of mixed design.

questions_now.q: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?
Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?

lines_now.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
lines_now.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where over 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and about half after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.
lines_now.rate: No fair test exists: the one death-rate study mostly compared later years with earlier ones in 19 Massachusetts towns, and the other studies only counted who survived, which can't show lives saved.

claim.statement: In communities where people who use heroin or other opioids, and others likely to witness an overdose, were trained to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and given naloxone to take home (an antidote that rapidly reverses the slowed breathing caused by opioids), the programmes are associated with lower opioid overdose death rates after statistical adjustment in the only study that compared death rates with years and places without them (mostly earlier years in the same communities), and most people given naloxone by a trained lay person survived; how many deaths the kits prevented is not known. In 19 Massachusetts cities and towns (Walley et al., 2013), chosen because each had at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, just before the programmes began, state-supported programmes of overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution enrolled 2,912 residents from September 2006 to December 2009 (2,007 who reported current drug use, treatment or recovery, and 905 others, typically social-service staff, family and friends), who reported 327 rescue attempts. Yearly opioid overdose death rates for 2002–2009 (poisoning deaths of unintentional or undetermined intent with an opioid-specific code or the narcotic code T40.6 on the death certificate, all opioids together) were compared between community-years with and without enrolment in a Poisson model with one linear time trend. No community had enrolment before 2006 and all 19 had it in 2008 and 2009, so the community-years without enrolment are all 19 communities in 2002–2005 and those not yet enrolling in 2006 and 2007 (12 and 5, by the editors' count): the comparison is mostly of later with earlier years in the same communities, although the introduction speaks of concurrent controls, and no communities outside the 19 were compared. With 1 to 100, and with more than 100 (more than 1 in 1,000 residents), cumulative enrolments per 100,000 residents, the death-rate ratios were 0.93 and 0.82 before adjustment (the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals) and 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76) after adjustment for community age, sex, race or ethnicity and poverty, rates of inpatient withdrawal treatment, methadone treatment and state-funded buprenorphine treatment, the share of opioid prescriptions dispensed to people obtaining schedule II opioid prescriptions from four or more prescribers and pharmacies, and year. In the article's second model, by enrolment below or above each year's median, the ratios were 0.85 and 1.00 before and 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90) and 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01) after adjustment, with no gradient, as the authors note; their abstract gives only the first model and calls the programmes an effective intervention, and their interpretation says the effect seemed dose-related. The unadjusted death rates plotted for community-years with enrolment are not consistently lower than those of 2002–2006 (Figure 1, the editors' approximate reading), so the size of the association depends on the adjustment, which includes the time trend. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together) was not associated with enrolment in either model (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00, every interval including 1); the authors suggest that bystanders calling for emergency help, as the training teaches, may balance out fewer overdoses, which was not tested (emergency services were called or present in 106 of 326 reported rescue attempts). The article prints no counts of deaths or hospital visits, no number of community-years in each group and no test for trend, so absolute differences cannot be given; analyses with cut-offs of 75 and 150 enrolments per 100,000, and with opioid overdose deaths divided by cancer deaths, are reported as similar without numbers and without a table (the online supplementary tables, which hold the control models, were not read), and its methods name 75 as the models' cut-off where its results and table use 100. The rescue attempts are trained bystanders' reports, collected when they asked for a naloxone refill: naloxone was reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts for which this was recorded, the 3 people it did not help received emergency care and survived, and the authors expect that rescues were under-reported. The authors state that their observational study cannot prove that the programmes caused the reduction (Walley et al., 2013). The study was funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with the first author as principal investigator and no role for the funder; the first author is listed as medical director of the Massachusetts opioid overdose prevention pilot, the trainers worked under a standing order from the programme's medical director, and three of the eight authors list the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, which expanded the programme and kept the programme database used for the enrolment counts; the competing-interests statement, which covers the previous three years, does not mention these roles. A systematic review of 22 observational studies published to June 2015 (McDonald & Strang, 2016: 15 in the USA, 2 in Canada, 4 in the UK and 1 in the UK and Germany; none randomized, two with a comparison group; eligibility, data extraction and quality rating by the first author under the supervision of the senior investigator), which includes the Massachusetts study, counted 2,336 naloxone administrations by trained lay people in 17 studies, after which 20 people were confirmed dead (0.9%), and at least 2,249 (96.3%) survived when 4 deaths with unclear naloxone use and 63 unknown outcomes are also counted as failures. These reversals, as the review calls them, count survival after naloxone, not deaths prevented: the review uses them as a stand-in because it cannot tell which overdoses would have been fatal without naloxone, and it cites a ratio of one fatal overdose in every 20 overdoses (editors' calculation: at that ratio, about 117 of 2,336 overdoses would have been expected to end in death; overdoses in which naloxone was used may have been more severe than most, so this only shows that survivals are not deaths prevented). In 21 of the 22 studies the overdose outcomes rested only on what participants reported, and in the 10 studies with unsystematic follow-up only 1,973 of 8,602 recipients (22.9%) are recorded as returning for a refill after using naloxone. The review judged that take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation, but its own results call the dose–response criterion only partly met and give the experimental-evidence criterion only preliminary support, both resting on the Massachusetts study alone, which is also the only included study that used death records; strength of association, biological plausibility and coherence rest on survival counts from 21 studies, consistency on reversals in at least 15 places, specificity on two cases, analogy on other emergency treatments given by lay people, and temporality on 21 studies in which training preceded reversals, among which the review singles out the Massachusetts study and an uncontrolled programme report from Chicago (fatal overdoses fell 20%, 8% and 6% in 2001–2003 after a 135% rise in 1996–2000), from which it says no definite conclusion can be drawn. The review describes the Massachusetts result as a fall compared with rates before implementation and with communities without the programme, and calls its dose relationship significant; in the full article, community-years without the programme exist only up to 2007, a gradient appears in only one of its two models, and no test for trend is printed. The review's abstract gives one death in 123 overdoses (0.8%, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) without saying that the figure comes from the nine studies with systematic follow-up, and the printed interval fits a denominator of 2,336, not 123 (editors' calculation: exact interval about 0.02% to 4.4%). The review notes that critics argue the observational data are not strong enough to infer that naloxone provision reduces deaths, and that overdose deaths in Australia fell during a heroin shortage in 2001–2002, before take-home naloxone was introduced there. Both review authors' employer holds intellectual property on a naloxone formulation, the second author (Strang) declares funding and payments from pharmaceutical companies, including work on naloxone products, and a patent registration for another naloxone formulation, and he co-wrote two of the included studies. Which drugs: all 22 studies reported mainly heroin overdoses, methadone was involved in fewer than 5% of reversals in the one study that reported it, and the review states that its results are limited to heroin overdoses and that effectiveness for long-acting opioids such as methadone or many prescription opioids is unclear; the Massachusetts deaths are counted for all opioids together, not by drug; neither source mentions fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: People who use opioids, mostly heroin, and potential bystanders (family members, peers and others likely to witness an overdose) trained by take-home naloxone programmes in the USA, Canada, the UK and Germany, in studies published to June 2015; for death rates, 19 Massachusetts cities and towns with at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, followed from 2002 to 2009, where 2,912 potential bystanders were trained in 2006–2009
claim.exposure: Overdose education with naloxone to take home (in Massachusetts, nasal naloxone): training to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and a naloxone kit; at community level, measured as cumulative programme enrolments per 100,000 residents (absolute model: none, 1 to 100, more than 100; relative model: none, below and above each year's median)
claim.comparator: Massachusetts: community-years without programme enrolment in the same 19 communities (all 19 in 2002–2005, 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007; none in 2008–2009), with regression adjustment including one linear time trend, and no communities outside the 19; review: for the survival counts, none (20 of the 22 studies had no comparison group)
claim.outcome: Rates of opioid-related poisoning death of unintentional or undetermined intent (Massachusetts death certificates, completed through a single statewide medical examiner office; all opioids together), and acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together); survival or death after naloxone given by a trained lay person, mostly as reported by participants (review)
claim.magnitude: Walley et al. (2013), full article: opioid overdose death-rate ratios against community-years without enrolment (all 19 communities in 2002–2005, and 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007 by the editors' count; none in 2008–2009), from Poisson models with one linear time trend (crude is the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals): absolute model, 1–100 enrolments per 100,000, crude 0.93, adjusted 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91), P<0.01; more than 100 per 100,000, crude 0.82, adjusted 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76), P<0.01; relative model, below each year's median, crude 0.85, adjusted 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90), P<0.01; above it, crude 1.00, adjusted 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01), P=0.06. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose, adjusted: 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) and 0.92 (0.75 to 1.13) in the absolute model, 0.90 (0.76 to 1.07) and 1.00 (0.86 to 1.16) in the relative model. 2,912 enrolled and 327 rescue attempts reported, 2006–2009; naloxone reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts with this recorded. No death or event counts, community-years per group or test for trend printed, so no absolute difference. McDonald & Strang (2016): 2,336 lay naloxone administrations in 17 studies; 20 confirmed deaths afterwards (0.9%, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), 24 including 4 with unclear naloxone use (1.0%, 0.6 to 1.4); at least 2,249 survivals (96.3%, 95.5 to 97.1); one death in 123 administrations in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (0.8%, printed 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2; editors' calculation: exact interval 0.02% to 4.4%); ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdoses cited (editors' calculation: about 117 of 2,336 expected deaths at that ratio). Deaths prevented: not known.
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an ecological time series in which most of the comparison is of later with earlier years in the same communities, through one linear time trend, and whose association is much weaker before adjustment; and survival counts without comparison) and one for indirectness (survival after naloxone stands in for deaths prevented; heroin, not fentanyl): very low. Rated as worded: an association between programme roll-out and lower opioid overdose death rates in one US state, and survival after naloxone given by trained lay people; the claim does not say that the kits prevented any number of deaths, which no study read could measure. Revisited after the full article of Walley et al. (2013) was read (the earlier versions rested on the BMJ's one-page print summary): the rating stays very low. The full article adds that all 19 communities had the programme in 2008–2009, that its second exposure model shows no gradient, that the unadjusted death rates it plots are not consistently lower with enrolment, that acute hospital care showed no association, and that no death counts are printed; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down two levels for the death-rate evidence, which would leave the certainty at very low, the lowest level. Overlap: the review includes the Massachusetts study, on which its dose–response and experimental-evidence judgments and its community-level mortality conclusion rest entirely, so the two sources are not independent for deaths. The review's other studies support that trained lay people used naloxone and that most people given it survived, not how many deaths were prevented; its judgment that all nine Bradford Hill criteria are met is reported as its judgment, with its own qualifications (dose–response only partly met, experimental evidence preliminary). Its abstract interval for one death in 123 is not used as printed (editors' recalculation in the statement). 'Is associated with', not 'reduces', at very low certainty (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: only one study compared death rates with a comparison. A review of fatal heroin overdoses in Victoria, Australia, listed in the project's harm-reduction list as a counter-case to take-home naloxone (Stam et al., 2018), is not on file; read it before this claim leaves draft.

questions_now.q: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?

lines_now.short: Feeling calm and ready beforehand went with easier trips; feeling anxious went with more anxiety.
lines_now.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. Feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people remembering their mood afterwards, and memories can be coloured by how the trip went.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
lines_now.rate: One online study of about 198 people planning their own trip, and one lab study. The online study lost about 70% of those who signed up and didn't allow for which drug people took.

claim.statement: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no named outcome measures or full measurement details, sample description or model details and its sample appears to overlap the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people who planned a psychedelic experience on their own initiative and signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in surveys
claim.exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
claim.comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study read here compared people helped to prepare with people who were not, and a systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 found none that compared different preparation, sets or settings
claim.outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
claim.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).
claim.rating_reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.

questions_now.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?
How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?

lines_now.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines_now.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.
lines_now.rate: One online survey of volunteers in 2016–17, who reported on themselves. Nobody checked hospital records or what they took, people who could not answer are missing, and only 19 described what happened.

freq.what: people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment afterwards
freq.note: Global Drug Survey 2017, online volunteers: 19 of 9,233 for magic mushrooms and 102 of 10,293 for LSD, all self-reported.

claim.statement: In people who had used magic mushrooms (mushrooms containing psilocybin) in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (12,534 respondents reported past-year use: 62.9% were under 25, 78.7% men, and most lived in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), 19 of the 9,233 who answered the question (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after using magic mushrooms in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (74% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 9,233 as the past-year group; among the 1,895 who completed the whole survey, 1,857 answered and 6 (0.3%) said yes, which the authors read as showing that most missing answers came from people who left the survey early. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 19 people by an estimated 34,347 days of use (a mean of 3.72 days a year), the authors put the figure at about 1 in 1,800 past-year intakes (0.06%). In the companion analysis of the same survey, 102 of 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year and answered (1.0%; about 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after LSD, which the authors describe as about five times the mushroom share (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022); per day of use, the LSD figure is about 3.4 times the mushroom figure (editors' calculation). Of the 19, 8 (42%) said they had been admitted to hospital, which the survey did not define (as the LSD paper states). They ticked a median of 5 symptoms from a list of 21: anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32% and seizures 26% (13, 13, 8, 7, 6 and 5 of the 19 by the editors' arithmetic, matching the bars of a figure that prints no values; in the same figure about 1 of the 19 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm); the authors note that passing out may in some cases have been brief memory loss or falling asleep, and that they cannot confirm that the seizures were epileptic rather than triggered by psychological factors. Of the 18 who said how long it took to feel back to normal, 17 did so within 24 hours (12 within 6 hours) and 1 within 5 to 7 days; the authors add that 'back to normal' may for some have meant only that the acute effects had resolved. In the session that led to emergency treatment, 8 of the 19 had taken nothing else and 11 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (7) or alcohol (6); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, with no 'other' option, they named their mood or mindset (9), mixing substances (7), the place or setting (7) or taking too much (5), or did not know (4); 1 thought the drug had not been magic mushrooms. The people who sought treatment were younger (median age 19 against 23; p = 0.002); with 19 events, no difference was detected by sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, usual quantity or frequency of use. Afterwards, 58% said they had cut down their use and 37% that it had not changed. The authors write that the results 'confirm psilocybin mushrooms are a relatively safe drug' and that harm-reduction information probably does much to prevent adverse effects; the survey cannot count deaths, lasting harm or people who could not or did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported magic mushroom use in the past 12 months (12,534; 62.9% under 25, 78.7% men, most living in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), of whom 9,233 answered the emergency-treatment question
claim.exposure: Use of magic mushrooms (psilocybin-containing mushrooms) in the past 12 months, self-reported; species, potency and content unknown; other substances in the incident session as reported
claim.comparator: None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, usual quantity and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used LSD
claim.outcome: Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after magic mushroom use in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 21, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use
claim.magnitude: Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al. (2022): 19 of 9,233 who answered (0.2%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.13% to 0.32%); completers 6 of 1,857 (0.3%); per day of use 0.00055 (0.06%, about 1 in 1,800; 19 divided by an estimated 34,347 days). Of the 19: hospital admission 8 (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%; editors' Wilson 23% to 64%); anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32%, seizures 26%; back to normal within 24 hours 17 of 18, within 5 to 7 days 18 of 18; nothing else taken 8, cannabis 7, alcohol 6; reasons mood or mindset 9, mixing 7, setting 7, too much 5, don't know 4, not magic mushrooms 1; median age 19 against 23 (p = 0.002). Companion LSD analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022): 102 of 10,293 (1.0%); editors' calculation: about 4.8 times the mushroom share per person and about 3.4 times per day of use.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use magic mushrooms and not a cause of the symptoms. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it. Status single study: one survey wave; the LSD figure comes from a companion analysis of the same survey by the same team and is a comparison within that survey, not a replication. The per-day figure is the authors' calculation and counts each person once. The authors' conclusions that the results confirm relative safety and that harm-reduction information plays a key role are not adopted: the survey could not count deaths or people who did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. Numbers of mushrooms are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.

questions_now.q: Can drug levels change after death?

lines_now.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall and differ between blood vessels.
lines_now.but: These studies cannot predict the change in one ordinary death.
how: Four selected overdose deaths showed large differences between blood vessels. A medicine given in hospital varied less.
In one person, all imipramine samples after death were about 2 to 8 times the earlier hospital level.
A collection of published reports and Finnish records found that the gap between body samples differs by drug.
Repeated tests found rises for some drugs and falls for others. The first sample was often taken hours after death.
lines_now.rate: Four overdose deaths picked as examples, and 5,375 cases gathered mostly from published reports, without showing how much results vary. Some evidence on changes after death comes from animals.

claim.statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 systemic vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about one hour before cardiac arrest (the reported intervals imply about two hours before death), every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributor and calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; the report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per body, alongside the separate sample from life in case 4 and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) calculated within-case ratios where a published source gave both values, then medians for each drug; the medians across these drug-specific medians were 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with more than tenfold ranges across the available drug-specific medians in all ten specimen types (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no within-drug range or interval is given, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the reported mean time to the first sample was about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. That summary is accompanied by 12 citations, but the review does not supply the underlying interval values, weights or aggregation method. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 99 entries (98 distinct labels), of which 82 have numeric parentheses, including an ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation; two are ranges and 16 labels, including THC, have no numeric value. It gives no case counts or per-value source attribution (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times the compilation's paired median for other blood. Other blood is not only heart blood, and the review's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; this comparison is descriptive, not a validated correction (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
claim.exposure: Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
claim.comparator: Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
claim.outcome: Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death
claim.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest systemic-blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold (excluding the separately reported portal values) per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

lines_now.short: In lab tests, strips found fentanyl in 104 of 106 drug samples that had it.
lines_now.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.
lines_now.rate: Teams in five labs agree. But the main check sorted 210 drug samples with a lab test that spots traces less well than the strip, so samples with only traces were left out.

freq.what: seized samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip
freq.note: 104 of 106 police-seized samples in which a lab machine had already found fentanyl. One brand, read by trained staff in two labs, 2017.

claim.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands, production lots and reading rules. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone. Because the forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS to find could enter this positive group, so how often strips miss samples with very little fentanyl was not measured (Green et al., 2020). Second-hand figures, relayed without their conditions, mostly point the same way: in British Columbia drug-checking data, 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples were missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024); and another paper relays 87.5 in 100 from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards prepared in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration, counting a faint test band as positive (the pictured strips at 25 and 50 ng/mL show a faint band, which the makers' rule, any visible band means negative, reads as negative; Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands in the main table, two of them with only a barely visible test band that the makers' rule reads as negative, and, in a descending series pictured for two brands, down to 50 and 25 ng/mL by the authors' rule (100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule), with no replicates reported and one brand graded differently at 100 ng/mL in the table and the figure (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL, from a heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024): a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Drug samples in laboratories: 210 police-seized samples from two US cities (2017), drug-checking samples in British Columbia (second-hand) and fentanyl reference standards dissolved in water or ethanol
claim.exposure: Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (mostly BTNX Rapid Response; four brands in one study), read by trained laboratory staff
claim.comparator: Earlier forensic GC/MS analysis of the same samples, or the known concentration of prepared solutions
claim.outcome: Whether the strip showed fentanyl when it was present (sensitivity), and the lowest fentanyl concentration it detected
claim.magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation); reference GC/MS limits 3.1 and 100 µg/mL. Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye, counting a faint band (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only, and in a pictured series down to 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL, heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024); 87.5% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al., 2022).
claim.rating_reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl in seized samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS and in pure solutions, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately, and the figure relayed by Klaire et al. is second-hand and not counted. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b) and adds one detection limit, from its heat sub-study.

questions_now.q: Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?
Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?

lines_now.short: Other drugs are often found. That does not show which caused the death.
lines_now.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours; other people were often present. These are findings relayed by a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers put 23 in 100 reported accidental drug-related deaths in categories beyond direct overdose, under their rules. Methadone was the only drug blamed in 4 in 100 direct overdoses; that does not mean no other drug was found.
Heroin exposure may also be missed when its marker breaks down. Blood levels also depend on the specimen and sampling time.
lines_now.rate: Old death records, mostly from 1967–1996, retold by a review that did not check its studies, plus one register from England and Wales in 2000. Neither describes today's drug supply.

claim.statement: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam was detected in 12% in one cited study; this is a diazepam-specific result, not sole exposure; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three publications about survivor comparisons without numerical results or enough detail to establish independent samples and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. These are recorded classifications. A ceiling for direct overdose and a floor for alternatives would be the editors’ conditional interpretation, assuming the other classifications were correct; neither is a validated bound on true causes or a measured error rate in official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The main death-series figures are historical and cannot describe current drug mixtures or yield a rate per use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Deaths attributed to heroin overdose by medical examiners, coroners or researchers in series from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly 1967–1996 (second-hand, Darke & Zador, 1996); 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to a national register in 2000 (Webb et al., 2003)
claim.exposure: Heroin use, shown by morphine (and where tested 6-MAM) found after death; other drugs found or named as implicated
claim.comparator: Morphine-only detection against co-detection; a Michigan series published 1977 comparing other-cause deaths (secondary); direct-overdose default category against alternative categories in England/Wales 2000
claim.outcome: What else was found in deaths attributed to heroin overdose, the timing and circumstances of death, and the mechanism of death
claim.magnitude: Secondary review: morphine-only 23%–48% across 6 series; alcohol 29%–75% across 13, mean 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; diazepam detected in 12% in one cited series, benzodiazepines 22%, 27%, 55% in 3 others. Correlations −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28. One series: a third below 0.16 mg/L, instant 14%, over 3 h 22%; other series over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52%; others present 58%–79%. Michigan paper published 1977: 74% no higher than comparison deaths. England/Wales 2000: 1,037; default direct-overdose classification 802/1,037=77.3% and alternatives 235/1,037=22.7% (editors’ calculations); any ceiling/floor interpretation assumes the other assignments were correct and is not a validated bound on true causes or official-statistics errors. Heroin/morphine implicated 424/802, detected 488/802; implicated 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related conditions, 11/18 infections. Alcohol co-detected 316/802=39.4%; methadone implicated 107/802≈13%, sole implicated 4% (sole implication, not sole detection). CSF comparison 46% more heroin-related cases, secondary and without counts; not deaths proved caused by heroin.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS§6.3); unchanged risk-of-bias and indirectness downgrades give very low. Replicated describes repeated co-detection/alternative mechanisms across historical series and a separate register, not replication of a causal share. The same primary series relayed by a review is counted once. Sole detection, sole implication and causal attribution remain distinct. Draft retained.
