questions_now.q: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?

lines_now.short: With the same therapy, PTSD scores fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.
lines_now.but: In the trial that asked, most people knew which pill they had.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Of those who finished, about 7 in 10 on MDMA no longer had PTSD, against 3 to 5 in 10 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA with standard talking therapy.
lines_now.rate: Two trials of 193 people in all, where chance decided who got MDMA. But most people probably knew which pill they had, and hope or disappointment could explain an unknown part of the difference.

claim.statement: In adults with moderate or severe PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines (two phase 3 trials from one sponsor: 90 adults with severe PTSD in MAPP1, 104 with moderate to severe PTSD in MAPP2), MDMA given in three sessions within an intensive manualized therapy, compared with an inactive placebo given with the same therapy, lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptom scores (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80, baseline means about 44 and 39) at 18 weeks by 11.9 points more in MAPP1 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 points more in MAPP2 (4.1 to 13.7); both arms improved substantially (in MAPP2, by 23.7 and 14.8 points). Analyses that kept scores recorded after people stopped treatment, a worst-case imputation of MAPP1's missing scores and a tipping-point analysis in MAPP2 still showed a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2's supplement). Among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2), 67% vs 32% and 71% vs 48% no longer met PTSD criteria; counting everyone randomized (for MAPP1, everyone dosed), 61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% (editors' calculation). Functional impairment improved slightly more with MDMA (SDS difference 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale in MAPP2, and 1.4 in MAPP1 by the amended study report as the sponsor's briefing document gives it). The two trials share their sponsor, design and therapy manual, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors; in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group at the end of the study, MAPP1 did not assess blinding, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, so how much of the difference is due to MDMA itself is uncertain; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, a single observational follow-up visit analysed in the FDA's briefing document, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability; no trial in the sources read compares MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused psychotherapy. The FDA's reviewers, re-tabulating the sponsor's study reports, give the same estimates and call the changes clinically meaningful (their threshold is 10 points), while judging that functional unblinding and expectation bias, which they cannot quantify, probably affected them, the in-session monitors probably knowing allocation too; the FDA's advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claim.population: Adults with DSM-5 PTSD of at least 6 months, CAPS-5 of 35 or more (MAPP1) or 28 or more (MAPP2), after washout of psychiatric medicines; people with current substance use disorders (MAPP1) or most substance use disorders (MAPP2), personality disorders or cardiovascular disease excluded, and in MAPP2 also people at high suicide risk
claim.exposure: MDMA in three 8-hour sessions about a month apart, within a manualized therapy of three preparatory and nine integration sessions with a two-person team
claim.comparator: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy
claim.outcome: Change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (primary); loss of PTSD diagnosis; SDS functional impairment
claim.magnitude: MAPP1 (de jure MMRM, n = 89): difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), d 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37) as printed (it equals the completers' raw difference of 10.5 points over their pooled SD; the model difference over the same SD gives about 1.03, editors' calculation); registry least-squares means −24.5 vs −12.64. MAPP2 (n = 103): −23.7 (−26.94 to −20.44) vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28); difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), d 0.7. Loss of diagnosis among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2): 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%) and 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); with everyone randomized as denominator (for MAPP1, the 46 and 44 dosed; editors' calculation): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 14.3 to 52.9) and 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8). Remission 14/42 vs 2/37 and 24/52 vs 9/42. SDS: MAPP2 difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14); MAPP1 P = 0.0116, d 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88) in the publication, but −1.36 (−2.46 to −0.25), P = 0.0167, in the FDA's table from the clinical study report. The FDA's tables give the same CAPS-5 estimates (MAPP2 P = 0.0004) and count 91 randomized in MAPP1 (46 and 45), of whom 90 were dosed; the sponsor's briefing document gives the same SDS difference. Sensitivity analyses (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2 supplement): MAPP1 de facto difference −12.04 (−17.46 to −6.62), worst-case imputation P = 0.0293; MAPP2 de facto −8.93 (−13.69 to −4.17); MAPP2 result significant until the missing placebo values are shifted 28 points toward improvement. Responder P values are nominal (MAPP2 response P = 0.0708).
claim.rating_reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (193 in the modified intention-to-treat sets, 90 and 103), starting high. Risk of bias, two levels (very serious): in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants very probably knew their group (in MAPP2's end-of-study survey 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it, mostly from effects felt or not felt; MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only anecdotes); neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, and the assessors' guesses were not recorded. This bias runs toward a larger difference (expectation on MDMA, disappointment on placebo, which the MAPP2 authors themselves name as a possible reason for the 8 vs 1 placebo dropouts, 5 of them after the first session); it is shared by both trials, so their agreement does not reduce it; and its size cannot be estimated from these papers, while the differences it would have to explain are of a comparable order (8.9 and 11.9 points, lower limits 4.1 and 6.3). METHODS §6.3 rates down when the biases that remain could plausibly change the estimate materially, as here (the FDA's reviewers reach the same view, add that the in-session monitors probably knew allocation too and say the bias cannot be quantified, and 9 of the 11 voting members of its advisory committee judged the data unable to show effectiveness); that the bias is unlikely to explain all of the difference argues against very low, not for moderate (the first reader's strict reading; both second readers). The sponsor's oversight of data collection, analysis and interpretation is carried by the status (replicated by the same team), not by a further level. Missing outcome data are not a further reason to rate down: analyses keeping scores recorded after people stopped treatment, MAPP1's worst-case imputation and MAPP2's tipping-point analysis all kept a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2 supplement); they do not address unblinding. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published. The relation stays 'reduces': randomization supports causal language about the package that was assigned (MDMA against placebo within the same therapy), which the site uses for randomized evidence at low certainty; how much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology is the question of the contested claim in section 14.

questions_now.q: Does psilocybin help depression?
Does psilocybin help depression?

lines_now.short: In two trials, depression scores fell more after one psilocybin session with two therapists than after a vitamin pill or a tiny dose. This was 3 to 6 weeks later.
lines_now.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.
lines_now.rate: Two trials where chance decided who got psilocybin. But people could probably tell whether they had it, nobody checked, and in one, many more dropped out of the vitamin-pill group.

freq.what: in the psilocybin group had their depression score at least halved at every check, week 1 to week 6
freq.note: One US trial of 104 adults: 20 of 48 against 5 of 44, counting only those checked at every visit.

claim.statement: In adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials, all off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing, one dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg, with preparation sessions beforehand, a supervised session of 6 to 10 hours with two therapists or facilitators, and integration sessions afterwards) compared with the same support and a 1-mg dose of psilocybin or a capsule of niacin is associated with larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 and 6 weeks later. In 233 adults with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode) at 22 sites in Europe and North America, 2019 to 2021, the MADRS (0 to 60) fell by 12.0 points after 25 mg, 7.9 after 10 mg and 5.4 after 1 mg by week 3, the primary end point: a difference of −6.6 points for 25 mg against 1 mg (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9), while 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg (−2.5, −6.2 to 1.2; P = 0.18) (Goodwin et al., 2022). Because the 10-mg comparison failed, the prespecified testing order stopped, so every secondary result, including those for 25 mg, counts formally as not significant: at week 3, 29 of 79 given 25 mg (37 in 100) and 14 of 79 given 1 mg (18 in 100) had responded (a fall of half or more), and 23 of 79 (29 in 100) and 6 of 79 (8 in 100) were in remission; a response kept from week 3 through week 12 was seen in 16 of 79 (20 in 100) against 8 of 79 (10 in 100) (odds ratio 2.2, 0.9 to 5.4). Between weeks 3 and 12, 26 of the 79 given 25 mg (33 in 100) started another treatment for depression, as did 16 of 79 given 1 mg. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation or self-injury from day 2 to week 3 occurred in 4 of 79 given 25 mg, 3 of 75 given 10 mg (besides 1 hospitalization for severe depression) and none of 79 given 1 mg; after week 3, suicidal behaviour in 3 given 25 mg (all with earlier suicidal behaviour or self-injury and no response at week 3), self-injury or suicidal ideation in 2 given 10 mg and self-injury in 1 given 1 mg (counts by period; the number of distinct people over the 12 weeks is not given). The trial was designed and funded by COMPASS Pathfinder, the company whose proprietary psilocybin formulation was tested, which also did the interpretation and post hoc analyses; 8 of the 74 authors are listed with the company, and the authors' disclosure forms are not printed in the article. In 104 adults with major depression (a current episode of at least 60 days; 13 of 104 met the trial's definition of treatment resistance) at 11 US sites, 2019 to 2022, scores fell by 19.1 points after psilocybin and 6.8 after niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical capsules, by day 43, the primary end point: a difference of −12.3 points (95% CI −17.5 to −7.2), with −12.0 by day 8 and no difference at day 2 (−0.1) (Raison et al., 2023; version corrected on 26 January 2024). Among those assessed at every visit, 20 of 48 assigned to psilocybin (42 in 100) and 5 of 44 assigned to niacin (11 in 100) kept a fall of half or more from day 8 to day 43, which the authors call a sustained response; sustained remission did not differ significantly (12 of 48 against 4 of 44; P = .05). By 6 weeks, 1 of 51 assigned to psilocybin and 9 of 53 assigned to niacin had withdrawn or been lost to follow-up. The authors call the reduction clinically significant, but no threshold for a meaningful difference was set in advance (they argue it afterwards from published values, using the point estimate; the interval reaches 7.2 points, below the 9 points they cite), 'sustained' means through day 43, and they state that the trial cannot show whether the effect would have faded later. No serious adverse events followed dosing and no suicidal or self-injurious behaviour was recorded; from the dosing day through day 9, adverse events judged related to the drug affected 41 of 50 given psilocybin (82 in 100) and 24 of 54 given niacin (44 in 100), and severe related events 4 of 50 and none. Some relative incidences and intervals printed for these adverse events do not fit their counts, so the counts are used (Raison et al., 2023). That trial was sponsored and funded by the Usona Institute, a non-profit medical research organization that supplied the psilocybin, designed the trial, interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript; 8 of the 35 authors are listed at the institute, and many authors report fees, grants or shares from companies developing psychedelic and other medicines. Neither trial checked whether participants could tell which they had received; both sets of authors say the acute effects of psilocybin probably weakened the blinding, and the Raison authors say this may have contributed to the effect and to the higher dropout with niacin. A two-page viewpoint on the Goodwin trial, with no data of its own, by an author of the Raison trial report who was not part of the Goodwin team (Gukasyan, 2023), singles out the missing blinding check as perhaps that trial's most serious flaw and argues that the suicidal behaviour of three participants given 25 mg, all with no response at week 3 and earlier suicide attempts or self-injury, should be taken seriously; events coded as suicidal behaviour were indeed all in the 25-mg group, but, as the trial's abstract states, suicidal ideation, behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, serious events included (counted above). The MADRS was rated by remote raters who did not know the group, from participants' own answers. Neither trial compared psilocybin with an established treatment or with an inert placebo; both excluded people judged to be at current risk of suicide and people with psychotic depression (Raison: any personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania), and most participants were White. These results describe psilocybin given in a medical trial with screening and psychological support, not use outside such settings. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: Adults with moderate to severe major depression in two randomized trials: 233 outpatients with treatment-resistant depression (no response to two to four adequate treatments in the current episode; episodes without psychotic features; mean age 39.8; 121 women; 215 White; 14 had used psilocybin before; mean baseline MADRS 32.5) at 22 sites in 10 countries in Europe and North America, March 2019 to September 2021 (Goodwin et al., 2022); and 104 medically healthy adults aged 21 to 65 with major depressive disorder (current episode of at least 60 days; central-rater MADRS of 28 or more at screening; 13 meeting the trial's definition of treatment resistance; median one earlier medicine in the current episode; mean age 41.1; 52 women; 89% White; mean baseline MADRS 35.5 and 35.0) at 11 US sites, December 2019 to June 2022 (Raison et al., 2023). All were off antidepressants for at least 2 weeks before dosing. Goodwin excluded people judged to be at clinically significant risk of suicide; Raison excluded active suicidal ideation with intent or plan, suicidal behaviour in the past 12 months, a personal or first-degree family history of psychosis or mania, moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder, and any psychedelic use in the past 5 years or more than 10 lifetime uses.
claim.exposure: One dose of psilocybin given by clinicians in the trial with psychological support (trial conditions: 25 mg of the proprietary synthetic formulation COMP360 in Goodwin et al., where 10 mg was also tested; 25 mg of synthetic psilocybin by mouth in Raison et al.), after preparation sessions (at least three therapist meetings; 6 to 8 hours with two facilitators), in a supervised session of 6 to 8 hours with two therapists (Goodwin) or 7 to 10 hours with two facilitators (Raison), followed by integration sessions
claim.comparator: The same preparation, session and integration with a 1-mg dose of the same psilocybin formulation (Goodwin et al., 2022) or with 100 mg of niacin, a vitamin that causes flushing, given as an active placebo in identical-looking capsules (Raison et al., 2023); no inert placebo and no established treatment
claim.outcome: Clinician-rated depression on the MADRS (0 to 60), rated by telephone by remote raters who did not know the group: change from baseline to week 3 (Goodwin, primary) and to day 43 (Raison, primary); response, remission and sustained response; dropout and starting other treatment; adverse events, including serious events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour
claim.magnitude: Goodwin et al. (2022), modified intention-to-treat (79, 75, 79): MADRS least-squares mean change to week 3 −12.0 (95% CI −14.6 to −9.3) with 25 mg, −7.9 (−10.6 to −5.2) with 10 mg, −5.4 (−8.1 to −2.7) with 1 mg; difference 25 mg against 1 mg −6.6 (−10.2 to −2.9), P<0.001; 10 mg against 1 mg −2.5 (−6.2 to 1.2), P = 0.18. Secondary, formally not significant because hierarchical testing stopped: response at week 3 29/79 (37%) against 14/79 (18%), odds ratio 2.9 (1.2 to 6.6); remission 23/79 (29%) against 6/79 (8%), 4.8 (1.8 to 12.8); sustained response to week 12 16/79 (20%) against 8/79 (10%), 2.2 (0.9 to 5.4). Editors' calculation (Wald): response difference 19.0 percentage points (5.4 to 32.5); remission 21.5 (9.9 to 33.1); sustained response 10.1 (−1.0 to 21.2); standardized difference for the primary contrast about 0.55 (SD about 11.9, back-calculated from the SE of the difference, 1.9). New depression treatment from week 3 to week 12: 26/79 (33%), 18/75 (24%), 16/79 (20%); before week 3: 4/79, 9/75, 14/79. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour: day 2 to week 3, 4/79, 3/75, 0/79; after week 3, 3/79, 2/75, 1/79 (by period). Raison et al. (2023), intention to treat (51, 53): MADRS change to day 43 −19.1 (−22.7 to −15.5) against −6.8 (−10.5 to −3.1), difference −12.3 (−17.5 to −7.2), P<.001; day 8 −12.0 (−16.6 to −7.4), P<.001; day 2 −0.1 (−2.1 to 1.9). Sustained response 20/48 (41.7%) against 5/44 (11.4%), difference 30.3 percentage points (13.5 to 47.1), odds ratio 5.60 (1.87 to 16.74), P = .002; sustained remission 12/48 (25.0%) against 4/44 (9.1%), odds ratio 3.37 (0.99 to 11.47), P = .05. claim.rating_reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down two levels for risk of bias (participants could very probably tell psilocybin from the control, which neither trial checked, with an outcome that rests on their own answers; the imputation in Goodwin and the uneven dropout in Raison run the same way): low. Rated as worded: larger falls in clinician-rated depression scores 3 weeks (Goodwin, treatment-resistant depression, against a 1-mg dose) and 6 weeks (Raison, mostly non-resistant depression, against niacin) after one 25-mg dose given with psychological support in trials. The claim does not say that the benefit lasts beyond 6 weeks (Goodwin's 12-week sustained response did not differ significantly, and a third of the 25-mg group had started other treatment by then), that 10 mg works (it did not differ from 1 mg), or how psilocybin compares with antidepressants (the separate answer on psilocybin against escitalopram). 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). The response and remission figures of Goodwin are formally not significant because the testing order stopped at the 10-mg comparison, and Raison's sustained response counts only participants assessed at every visit; both are reported as such. Raison's printed relative incidences for related, mild and moderate adverse events do not fit their counts and are not used. Status replicated: two trials with different sponsors, formulations, populations and lead teams point the same way; they share one site (Emory University, Atlanta) and two of its investigators (B. W. Dunlop; T. Mletzko, listed as Mletzko-Crowe in Goodwin) among 22 and 11 sites, which the editors do not count as the same team; the second reader should confirm. Funding and the authors' ties are given as each paper prints them; Goodwin's disclosure forms are not printed and were not read. One published response to Goodwin et al. is now on file: a two-page viewpoint without data of its own (Gukasyan, 2023), by an author of the Raison trial report who declares a co-investigator role on a psilocybin study funded by the Usona Institute (Raison et al., 2023, pp. 843, 851–852). Its two concerns, the missing blinding check and suicidality, are already in the statement and in the rating (risk of bias down two levels), so it changes neither the certainty nor the status. Its framing was checked against the trial's counts (Goodwin et al., 2022, pp. 1637, 1644–1645): events coded as suicidal behaviour (3 participants after week 3) were all in the 25-mg group, as the viewpoint says, but suicidal ideation or behaviour or self-injury occurred in every dose group, as the trial's abstract states, and worsening of suicidal state by week 3 was most frequent with 10 mg (13 of 75, against 11 of 79 with 25 mg and 7 of 79 with 1 mg); the trial places the suicidal behaviour after week 3, without the one to two months the viewpoint gives, and the viewpoint calls the adverse events relatively high without figures (66 of 79, 56 of 75 and 57 of 79). Published critiques of Raison et al. are not on file; the rating should be revisited when they are (METHODS §2.3).

questions_now.q: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?
Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?

lines_now.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines_now.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: DARE was one of the most used US school drug programmes; the review's authors cite spending of about three quarters of a billion dollars yearly.
A 2004 review combined 11 studies, from 1991 to 2002, comparing students who had DARE with students who didn't.
Students who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as others, from right after the classes to 10 years later.
Two small studies found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more. Four results were filled in as zero.
lines_now.rate: One short review of 11 school studies of the original DARE classes. It did not check how well the studies were done and filled in four results as zero, so its numbers are rough.

claim.statement: In school students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given; the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme), in 11 controlled evaluations published in journals between 1991 and 2002 (236 to 2,878 students each, 11,505 listed in all, editors' sum; experimental and quasi-experimental designs, the review not saying which were which), the original Project D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education) school curriculum compared with each study's control or comparison condition does not detectably change self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, measured from immediately after the programme to 10 years later: pooled d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; r = 0.011; z = 0.73, not significant), below the level usually considered small (West & O'Neal, 2004; no funding statement). In 8 of the 11 studies the interval included no difference (editors' count from Table 1); the largest, of 2,878 fifth graders, found slightly more use in the D.A.R.E. group (d = −0.117, −0.19 to −0.04), and two small studies found less (395 sixth graders, d = 0.376, 0.07 to 0.68; 236 fifth and sixth graders, smoking the only outcome, d = 0.405, 0.01 to 0.80). Four of the 11 effects, covering 4,539 of the 11,505 students listed (39%, editors' sum) and including the only 10-year follow-up, were not computed but entered as zero and footnoted as assumed. The review did not appraise its studies, names no pooling model and reports no heterogeneity; a random-effects pooling of its printed values reproduces its estimate, while a fixed-effect pooling gives d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034), so the near-zero result does not depend on the model (editors' recalculation; study estimates vary more than chance would predict, I² about 54%). Many included studies analysed individual students although students were nested in schools, which the authors say tends to overestimate effectiveness and judge unlikely to change the result; ignoring the clustering also makes the pooled interval narrower than it should be (editors' note). Every study evaluated the original curriculum: D.A.R.E. was substantially revamped in 2001, and the authors found no evaluation of the new version, so this answer does not apply to it. The authors' remark that the effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to count as small overstates the gap: Cohen's small benchmarks are about 9 times the pooled values (editors' calculation). An earlier meta-analysis, as the paper describes it, found negligible effects (0.00 to 0.11) immediately after the programme. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: School students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given in the review, which presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme; 236 to 2,878 per study; 11,505 listed across the 11 studies, editors' sum) in 11 controlled evaluations (experimental or quasi-experimental, not distinguished in the review) published in peer-reviewed journals from 1991 to 2002
claim.exposure: The original Project D.A.R.E. school curriculum, before its 2001 revision; content, number of sessions and delivery not described in the review
claim.comparator: Each study's control or comparison condition, not described in the review
claim.outcome: Self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, from immediately after the programme to 10 years later
claim.magnitude: West & O'Neal (2004): pooled r = 0.011, d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; the interval is on the d scale, editors' check), z = 0.73, not significant; positive values favour D.A.R.E. Study effects (Table 1): Becker 1992 d = −0.117 (−0.19 to −0.04; 2,878 students); Zagumny & Thompson 1997 d = 0.376 (0.07 to 0.68; 395); Ahmed 2002 d = 0.405 (0.01 to 0.80; 236; smoking only); four effects entered as assumed zeros (Ennett 1994, Rosenbaum 1994, Wysong 1994, Lynam 1999; 4,539 of 11,505 students, 39%, editors' sum); 8 of 11 intervals include zero (editors' count). Editors' recalculation from the printed d values and intervals: random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) d = 0.023 (−0.039 to 0.085), reproducing the published estimate; fixed-effect d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Q = 21.6 on 10 df (P about 0.02), I² about 54%. Cohen's small benchmarks (d = 0.2, r = 0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled values (editors' calculation), against the paper's 20 times. No absolute difference in the share of students using any substance can be given.
claim.rating_reasoning: The review admitted experimental and quasi-experimental designs without saying which studies were randomized, so the evidence cannot be treated as randomized and starts low; seen only through this review, which did not appraise its studies, it is rated down one level for risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), giving very low, the floor. Rated as worded: no detectable effect of the original curriculum on self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs combined; the pooled effect is near zero (d = 0.023) with an interval that excludes Cohen's small benchmark, and a fixed-effect pooling gives −0.005 (editors' recalculation). The very low rating reflects how little this single brief review lets anyone check (designs not reported, four effects assumed, clustering ignored), not a sign of a hidden benefit: the biases expected in such studies would favour D.A.R.E. The authors' remark that the effect would need to be 20 times larger to count as small is not adopted (about 9 times, editors' calculation). Status replicated: the review reports each study's direction, and in 8 of 11 independent evaluations the interval included no difference; the earlier meta-analysis, described in the paper but not read, agrees and is not counted. The answer does not cover the curriculum revised in 2001.

questions_now.q: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?
How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?

lines_now.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines_now.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.
lines_now.rate: Two large US surveys, a decade apart, give almost the same figure. But they asked people in their homes between 1990 and 2005, so other countries and today's cannabis may differ.

freq.what: of people who had ever used cannabis had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey of people aged 15 to 54, 1990 to 1992, with an older, narrower definition of dependence; the tobacco figure was worked out from two surveys.

claim.statement: In two US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had met, or were estimated to meet at some time in their life, criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey and 31.9% for tobacco (tobacco dependence was assessed, for daily smoking only, in a subsample of 4,414 and divided by tobacco use taken from another 1991 national survey, so it has no standard error); among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, and half of the people who became dependent had done so within about 5 years of first use; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. Two of these reviews also give about 1 in 10 for other groups without data of their own: Connor et al. (2021), citing a UN report, for people who use cannabis worldwide and for people who use it regularly, and Hall (2015), in its abstract, for people who use it regularly. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). Higher figures from more recent US national data use other definitions and denominators: Connor et al. (2021) cite about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and a 2020 professional statement gives 3 in 10 people who had used cannabis in the past year as meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis of the 2012 to 2013 survey; second-hand); the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claim.population: People in US national household surveys who had ever used cannabis: ages 15 to 54 in 1990 to 1992 (National Comorbidity Survey; 46.3% of 8,098 had used) and adults interviewed in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005 (NESARC; 7,389 who had used)
claim.exposure: Any lifetime use of cannabis, even once (in the 1990-92 survey the dependence questions were asked only after at least several occasions of use)
claim.comparator: None for the main figure (a share of everyone who had used); other substances in the same surveys
claim.outcome: Lifetime DSM-III-R cannabis dependence as a proportion at interview (1990-92); lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV cannabis dependence after first use, by years since first use (2001-05)
claim.magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); tobacco 31.9% (no SE: dependence assessed in a subsample of 4,414, use taken from the 1991 NHSDA); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; half of the cases of dependence about 5 years after first use (a median among people who became dependent). Second-hand: about 1 in 10 of people who use regularly (Connor et al., 2021, citing a UN report; Hall, 2015, abstract); about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015); 3 in 10 people who used in the past year meeting criteria for a use disorder (Page et al., 2020, citing a 2016 analysis).
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions in survey populations): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: two independent national probability surveys, a decade apart and with different instruments and DSM versions, give about 9 in 100, and the claim states their measures, years and populations. Strict reading: the 2001-05 timing figures (5.9% within 10 years, about 2% in the first year, half of the cases within about 5 years) rest on recalled ages and an actuarial curve without intervals and on their own would be rated down one level for risk of bias, to very low. The narrative reviews and the 2020 professional statement are used only to trace the figure they repeat, to show the other denominators behind higher figures, and for the DSM-5 definition; they add no data, and the 30% and 3 in 10 they cite for newer data are second-hand and on other denominators and do not enter the rating. Overlap: Hall & Degenhardt (2009), Hall (2015) and Connor et al. (2021) take their 9% from the 1990-92 survey or a chapter by its first author (Connor's other 1 in 10 figures come from a UN report), and Volkow et al. (2014) and Curran et al. (2016) from the 2001-05 analysis, so the reviews are not further replication. Status replicated: the two surveys are independent and agree.

questions_now.q: Can people become dependent on ecstasy?

lines_now.short: Some people become dependent on ecstasy. Studies disagree on how many.
lines_now.but: Most studies used volunteers and survey forms made for other drugs, so the numbers may not fit everyone.
how: In two US national surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. In club-goer, detention and volunteer samples, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

Tolerance means needing more for the same effect. It was among the symptoms people reported most, and it went with using more, or for longer, than meant. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.
lines_now.rate: Studies of 26 to 1,662 people, seen only through one 2010 overview. Who was asked shaped the answer, from 3.6 to 73 in 100, and pills sold as ecstasy may not be MDMA.

claim.statement: As summarized by a 2010 narrative review (Degenhardt, Bruno, et al., 2010), studies of people who use ecstasy have found that some meet criteria for dependence, but the share ranges from about 4 in 100 to 73 in 100 depending on who was asked, how, and over what period. In two US household surveys, 3.6 in 100 people who had used ecstasy in the past year (Wu et al.) and 3.8 in 100 of those who had started within the previous two years (Stone et al.) met criteria for hallucinogen dependence. In a German community study, 0.4 in 100 of all young adults met past-year criteria for ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence, and 5.8 in 100 of people who had ever used ecstasy had ever met criteria (about 12 of 207 people, by our arithmetic from the table). In samples recruited differently, 19 in 100 of New York nightclub attendees and 22 in 100 of Taiwanese juvenile detainees who used ecstasy met past-year criteria, and 16 to 18 in 100 in convenience samples in Germany, the UK and Australia (195, 1,106 and 1,662 people) were counted as dependent or scored above a screening scale's cut-off. The highest figures, 43, 64 and 73 in 100 over a lifetime, came from three small samples: 52 adolescents and young adults in drug treatment and in the community who had used ecstasy at least 5 times, 185 people the review describes as regularly using ecstasy, and 59 rave attendees who had taken at least 250 tablets in their lifetime. The review says all the instruments were designed for other drugs, only one study used a clinician's assessment, assessment was mostly by self-report and lifetime recall, and most samples were recruited by convenience or snowball methods, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy; it adds that people often reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use and that it is unclear whether they understood the questions as intended, and that pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some dependence may be on another drug. Across studies, the symptoms most often reported included continued use despite problems, spending a lot of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal; in two studies the symptoms fell into a group about compulsive use and a group about escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended). In the one study that followed people (the German community study above), 93 in 100 of those who met criteria at the start no longer did just over three years later and 50 in 100 had stopped using ecstasy altogether; the review does not give the size of that group, which by our arithmetic was about 12 to 14 people. In Australia, fewer than 1 in 100 treatment episodes were for ecstasy. The review also describes animal studies in which MDMA is rewarding but may be less so than other illicit drugs, and notes a lack of case reports of severe withdrawal. It concludes that the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is thin in scope and design.
claim.population: People who use ecstasy in studies summarized by a 2010 narrative review: US and German general-population surveys, New York nightclub attendees, Taiwanese juvenile detainees, and convenience samples in Australia, Germany, the UK and the US (26 to 1,662 people per study)
claim.exposure: Use of ecstasy (pills sold as ecstasy, contents not tested), from a few lifetime occasions to hundreds of tablets
claim.comparator: None in most studies; one study compared ecstasy with other hallucinogens; one followed people over time
claim.outcome: Meeting criteria for dependence on questionnaires or interviews designed for other drugs (DSM-IV hallucinogen or amphetamine criteria, CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale and others), past year, past month or lifetime
claim.magnitude: Share meeting criteria, as printed in Table 1: general population: 3.8% past year (Stone, N 1199, people who started within 2 years), 3.6% past year (Wu, N 652; text says 4%, another 11% with one or two symptoms), 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy (von Sydow, N 207; about 12 people, editors' arithmetic) with 0.4% of all young adults dependent in the past year; sentinel samples: 19% past year (Parsons, N 214), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, N 200); self-selected or convenience samples: 18% past month (Bruno, N 1662, scale cut-off 4 or more), 17% (Winstock, N 1106, scale cut-off 5 or more, timeframe not specified in the table, lifetime in the text), 16% (Tossman, N 195, timeframe not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, N 154, probable dependence), 43% lifetime (Cottler, N 52), 64% lifetime (Topp, N 185), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, N 59, at least 250 lifetime tablets, clinician-rated); Hanson and Luciana (N 26): prevalence cell N = 2 but 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the details column and text. Course (von Sydow, just over 3 years): 93% no longer dependent, 50% no longer using, 43% still using (group size not given; editors' arithmetic: about 12 to 14 people). Treatment: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes. No intervals are given.
claim.rating_reasoning: Descriptive prevalence from observational studies starts low (METHODS 6.3); each of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision takes a level, so the result is very low. That some people meet criteria is better supported than any one percentage. Status replicated in direction only: every study finds some people meeting criteria, while the size varies widely, as the claim states (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim reports findings, makes no statement about risk for any one person and gives no advice.

questions_now.q: Is low blood salt after MDMA more common in women?

lines_now.short: Women with MDMA illness more often had low blood salt than men did.
lines_now.but: These are people who became ill and had a blood test, not everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Of 105 women with a blood salt test, 55 (52 in 100) had a low level; of 83 men, 18 (22 in 100) did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.

A review describes one controlled study in 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount. A hormone marker rose only in the women; the review does not identify the comparison behind its other hormone and sodium results. This does not establish why women were more common in the reported cases.
lines_now.rate: Records of 188 people at one California poison centre who had blood salt measured. Body size and other differences between women and men were not recorded or allowed for.

claim.statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA (study condition; the review does not specify the setting), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were reported in the hormone itself or in blood sodium; the review does not identify that statistical contrast, so it cannot be treated as a demonstrated absence of a sex difference. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 female rows among 52 (88.5 in 100 by editorial calculation, whereas the review prints 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (conditionally 44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation, not a verified unique-patient count), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
claim.population: People with ecstasy intoxication reported to the California Poison Control System in 2000 to 2005 and given a serum sodium result: 188 of 545 included cases (105 women, 83 men; mean age 21 in both); descriptively, 17 UK patients aged 15 to 26 and published case reports tabulated in two narrative reviews; and, as described in the 2020 review, 16 healthy volunteers (8 women, 8 men) in one laboratory study
claim.exposure: Female sex, among people who took ecstasy (MDMA) and became ill; amounts of MDMA and of fluid not recorded
claim.comparator: Men with a recorded sodium; within each sex, people with low sodium against people without
claim.outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L; coma and seizure among those with and without low sodium
claim.magnitude: California poison control, people with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded sodium (Rosenson): low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) in 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%), odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); of the 73 with low sodium, 55 (75.3%) were women, against 296 of 545 (54.3%) women among all cases. Sodium was recorded in 35.3% of women and 33.3% of men. Within each sex, low sodium against not: coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Editors' calculation: 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium among those tested (52.4 minus 21.7). UK series (Hartung): 10 of 17 patients and both deaths female. Earlier series cited by the California paper (not read): 17 of 18 women; 2 of 3 in an Israeli series of 32. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 85% of published symptomatic cases female. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: 46 of 52 rows female (88.5%, editors' calculation; review prints 89%; conditionally omitting two probable duplicates gives 44/50=88.0%, not a verified unique-patient count); controlled crossover, 8 men and 8 women given 125 mg MDMA: copeptin rose in women but not in men, no significant ADH/sodium differences reported, statistical contrast unspecified; postoperative patients with hyponatraemic encephalopathy (Ayus et al., 1992): menstruant women about 25 times as likely to die or have permanent brain injury as men or postmenopausal women. No rate in women or men who take MDMA can be derived.
claim.rating_reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference among reported cases; the UK series and the two reviews are consistent but do not test it, and both reviews' tables overlap the California series. The 2020 review (Faria et al.; card sc_faria_2020) infers a female predisposition from its case counts, but its table has errors and no denominators, and the only controlled comparison it describes (Simmler et al., 2011, not read) reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the statistical contrast; that study and the postoperative data (Ayus et al., 1992, not read) are second-hand. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.
